title: A Strongly Subcubic Combinatorial Algorithm for Triangle Detection with Applications

predicted_errors.error_location: Correctness analysis, Case 2.1 ("Exactly one vertex, namely a, appears on level 1")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof asserts that if s ∈ N(a) and only a of T = {a,b,c} is on level 1, then b and c appear on level 2 and "the triangle {a,b,c} is detected while scanning the adjacency list of b". This does not follow: b and c may be discovered from *different* level-1 vertices (b from some other neighbor d of s, c from a). The only triangle-revealing tests that a BFS can do in O(1) per edge are edges to the BFS parent or edges between two vertices with the same parent; when parent(b) ≠ parent(c) the edge bc gives no information that a is adjacent to both b and c, so the triangle is not detected. Hence the key claim "if s ∈ A then BFS⁺(s) finds a triangle" — on which the whole O(n^{7/3}) result (and every downstream theorem) rests — is unproven/false as argued. Verifying the needed condition in general would also break the claimed O(m) cost per BFS.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section describing TRIANGLE-DETECTION-1 ("See Step 12 of the modified BFS procedure")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The algorithm BFS⁺ — the subroutine on which both the correctness argument ("Step 12") and the O(m) per-call running time depend — is never specified anywhere in the text. The paper repeatedly refers to 'Step 12 of the modified BFS procedure' and to figures, but no pseudocode or precise description of the triangle test performed during BFS is given, making the correctness and timing claims unverifiable as stated.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction ("the greatest advance in triangle detection in over 45 years and the greatest advance in Boolean matrix multiplication in over 50 years")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claimed BMM bound is Õ(n^{25/9}) ≈ n^{2.778}, which is *slower* than the long-known FMM-based BMM running in O(n^ω) = O(n^{2.372}) that the paper itself cites. Likewise the triangle bound n^{7/3}=n^{2.333} improves the FMM bound only in the fourth decimal of the exponent. Describing these as 'the greatest advance ... in over 50 years' is a rhetorical overstatement not supported by the reported numbers (the advance, if correct, is only within the class of combinatorial algorithms).

predicted_errors.error_location: k-clique application ("if k = 100 ... whereas the previous record was O(n^100 / polylog(n))")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Earlier in the same section the paper states that the fastest k-clique algorithm (Nešetřil–Poljak) runs in O(n^{0.791k}), i.e. O(n^{79.1}) for k=100. Calling O(n^{100}/polylog n) 'the previous record' contradicts this; that bound is only the record among combinatorial algorithms, and the qualifier is omitted.

The same paper (A. Abboud and V. V. Williams, 'Popular conjectures imply strong lower bounds for dynamic problems') is listed twice, once as the FOCS 2014 version [4] and once as arXiv:1402.0054 [5]; [4] is never cited in the text while Lemma 1 is attributed only to [5]. Duplicate/ghost references of this kind need correction.

predicted_errors.error_location: Applications section, K_6 paragraph ("O(n^{4.751}) or O(m^{2.372})") and K_4 paragraph ("O(m^{(ω+1)/2}) = O(m^{1.687})")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states ω < 2.372 throughout; then the K_6 bound n^{2ω} should be O(n^{4.744}), not O(n^{4.751}) (4.751 corresponds to the older value ω ≈ 2.3755), and (ω+1)/2 = 1.686, not 1.687. The exponents quoted are internally inconsistent with the value of ω adopted in the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Witness-matrix discussion ("computes a matrix of witnesses in time O(n^ω log n); if ω = 2, the runtime becomes O(n^2 log^2 n)")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Substituting ω = 2 into O(n^ω log n) gives O(n^2 log n), not O(n^2 log^2 n). The two statements in the same sentence are mathematically inconsistent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Applications section ("the fastest known algorithm for detecting a K_4, due to Alon, Yuster, and Zwick, runs in O(n^{ω+1})")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The O(n^{ω+1}) bound for K_4 detection comes from the Nešetřil–Poljak scheme (and is discussed by Eisenbrand–Grandoni [18]); Alon, Yuster and Zwick's cited papers [8,9] concern color-coding and finding/counting cycles, not an O(n^{ω+1}) K_4 algorithm. The attribution is incorrect.
SODA 2021 is the 32nd ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms, not the 31st (SODA 2020 was the 31st); the bibliographic entry is inconsistent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Paragraph preceding Theorem 3 ("the above statement had until now more of a speculative nature")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Williams–Williams subcubic equivalence between triangle detection and BMM is a proved theorem; describing it as 'speculative' because no subcubic combinatorial algorithm was known mischaracterizes an established result (only the realizability of one of its two alternatives was open).

predicted_errors.error_location: Probability analysis ("by applying the standard inequality 1 − x ≤ e^{−x} for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1/2. Indeed, we have x/n ≤ 1/2 for n ≥ 4")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The inequality 1 − t ≤ e^{−t} holds for all real t, so the stated range restriction is spurious; moreover the justification 'x/n ≤ 1/2 for n ≥ 4' is not established, since x = ⌊m^{1/3}⌋ depends on m and the claim is asserted without argument (it needs m ≤ n^3/8). The argument as written is sloppy/incorrect reasoning even though the final bound happens to hold.
